title: Behind the Headline: How News Is Written
paragraphs: Open any international newspaper and count the passive constructions on the front page. The exercise is instructive: on a typical day, you will find that between a third and a half of all clauses in news writing use passive voice. "Three people were killed." "The building was destroyed by fire." "A new policy has been announced." "The suspects are being questioned." These are not stylistic accidents — they are the deliberate choices of writers who understand exactly when the passive serves communication better than the active.

The passive is the natural choice in news writing for several structural reasons. First, news stories are almost always focused on the event or its victim, not the agent. When a building burns down, the building is the news — not the fire. "The building was destroyed" puts the building first, which is where reader attention belongs. "Fire destroyed the building" puts fire first, which shifts attention away from the more newsworthy subject.

Second, in breaking news, the agent is often unknown. "A bomb has been detonated in the city centre" is more factually accurate than "someone has detonated a bomb in the city centre" — because at the time of writing, no one knows who detonated it. The passive allows journalists to report the event without overstating what is known. This is not evasion — it is precision.

Third, the passive allows what linguists call "topic continuity." When a news story follows a particular subject through a sequence of events, keeping that subject in topic position throughout — "he was arrested, was charged, was released on bail, and has since been placed under surveillance" — creates coherence and readability that active voice would disrupt.

The get passive is less common in formal news writing but appears in more conversational journalistic genres — blogs, comment pieces, human interest stories. "She got fired after posting a photo online." "The candidates got selected through a genuinely competitive process." "The deal got done in the early hours of the morning." The get passive typically emphasises the subject's experience of the event — often with overtones of surprise, inconvenience, or fortune.

Academic and scientific writing follows similar principles. When researchers report experimental findings, the passive is the standard: "Samples were collected. The data was analysed. The hypothesis was supported." This is not because passive sounds more prestigious — it is because the researcher's identity is genuinely irrelevant to the findings. What matters is not who collected the samples but that they were collected, and in what way.

Understanding these conventions is not just useful for writing — it is essential for reading critically. When passive voice hides the agent, ask why. When a press release says "mistakes were made," notice what is missing. When a company states that "a decision has been taken to reduce the workforce," the passive is doing political work: it reports the decision without attaching it to a decision-maker. Passive voice is a tool. Like all tools, it can be used honestly or dishonestly.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I've been trying to write more passively in my academic essays. But I'm not sure when to use it.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Think about what you want to focus on. Passive puts the object or result first — the action, not the actor.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: So in my economics essay, should I say "the government implemented the policy" or "the policy was implemented by the government"?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: What are you writing about — the government or the policy?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Then passive: "The policy was implemented." The government isn't the point — the policy is. You don't even need "by the government" if it's obvious.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: And when someone gets fired, is that "get passive"?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Yes. "She got fired" emphasises what happened to her — it's more experiential. "She was fired" is more neutral.

keyPhrases.context: "In breaking news, the agent is often unknown." = news being reported as it happens.
"Topic continuity." = keeping the same subject throughout a sequence of sentences.
"The agent is unknown." = the person or thing performing the action.
"This is not evasion — it is precision." = using passive to be accurate, not to hide.
"Journalistic genres." = types or categories of writing with their own conventions.
"Without overstating what is known." = reporting facts without exaggerating certainty.
"Creates coherence and readability." = logical connection between parts of a text.
"Understanding these conventions." = accepted ways of doing things in a particular field.

vocab.example: "These are not accidents — they are the deliberate choices of skilled writers."

vocab.definition: the person or thing performing the action in a sentence
vocab.example: "Fire destroyed the building." — fire is the agent. In passive, the agent may be omitted.

vocab.definition: the quality of forming a logical and consistent whole
vocab.example: "Passive creates coherence and readability." — parts connect logically.

vocab.definition: the act of avoiding something, especially a question or responsibility
vocab.example: "This is not evasion — it is precision." — not hiding, just accurate reporting.

vocab.definition: a subtle quality or implication beyond the main meaning
vocab.example: "Get passive has overtones of surprise or inconvenience."

vocab.definition: close observation or monitoring of a person or place
vocab.example: "He has been placed under surveillance." — passive + state result.

vocab.definition: all the people engaged in or available for work
vocab.example: "A decision has been taken to reduce the workforce." — passive hides the decision-maker.
"The exercise is instructive." — counting passive constructions teaches you about news writing.
